AR and ARMA error correction, explained

pdmS7 documentation

Source: vignettes/ar-error-correction.Rmd
ar-error-correction.Rmd

A rainfall-runoff model is never exactly right, and its errors are not random from one time step to the next. If the model is 2 m3/s low now, it will very probably be about 2 m3/s low in 15 minutes’ time too. Error correction uses that. At the moment a forecast is issued, the latest error is known, because the river has been measured. An autoregressive (AR) model predicts how that error will carry on, and the forecast becomes the simulation plus the predicted error.

This is what IMFS does operationally, as post-processing on top of the model. This article explains, in plain terms, what the AR coefficients mean, where they come from, and where the method stops working. Testing forecasts with hindcasts shows how to measure whether it helps on your catchment.

Why errors persist

A made-up catchment at 15-minute steps, with a model whose rainfall factor is 10 per cent low and whose stores are a little too fast:

set.seed(5)
n <- 4 * 24 * 60
wet <- stats::runif(n / 16) < 0.12
rain <- rep(ifelse(wet, stats::rgamma(n / 16, 0.8, scale = 2.5), 0), each = 16) / 4
forcing <- data.frame(rain = rain, pet = 0.01)
truth <- pdm_model(area_km2 = 60, fc = 1.1, dt = 0.25,
                   surface = FlodeCascadeRouting(k1 = 3, k2 = 5))
model <- pdm_model(area_km2 = 60, fc = 1.0, dt = 0.25,
                   surface = FlodeCascadeRouting(k1 = 2, k2 = 4))
observed <- run_pdm(truth, forcing, initial_state_from_flow(truth, 1, 0.7))$output$q_m3s *
  exp(stats::rnorm(n, 0, 0.01))
simulated <- run_pdm(model, forcing, initial_state_from_flow(model, 1, 0.7))$output$q_m3s
error <- observed - simulated

The error is observed minus simulated, so a positive error means the model is too low. This is the convention of IMFS and reach.postproc.

days <- (n - 4 * 24 * 10 + 1):n
hours <- (days - days[1]) / 4
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(hours, observed[days], pch = 16, cex = 0.2, col = pal[1], xlab = "", ylab = "Flow (m3/s)")
lines(hours, simulated[days], col = pal[2], lwd = 1.5)
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(hours, error[days], type = "l", col = pal[3], lwd = 1.5, xlab = "Hours",
     ylab = "Error (m3/s)")
abline(h = 0, col = pal[7], lty = 2)

Top: observed (points) and simulated (line) flow over ten days. Bottom: the error.

The error moves slowly: it builds up during a flood and drains away afterwards. Measured over the whole record, the error now and the error 15 minutes later have a correlation of 0.995; one hour apart, 0.959; six hours apart, still 0.30. That memory is what an AR model exploits.

The simplest case: one coefficient

An AR(1) model says the next error is a fixed fraction of the current one:

next error = a × current error

With a = 0.9, an error of 1 m3/s is predicted to be 0.9 after one step, 0.81 after two, and so on: it fades away, more slowly the closer a is to 1. With a = 1 it would never fade, which is the same as assuming the model stays exactly as wrong as it is now.

project <- function(a, start, steps) {
  e <- start
  out <- numeric(steps)
  for (k in seq_len(steps)) {
    out[k] <- sum(a * e)
    e <- c(out[k], e[-length(e)])
  }
  out
}
steps <- 4 * 48
lead <- seq_len(steps) / 4
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(range(lead), c(0, 1), type = "n", xlab = "Lead time (h)", ylab = "Predicted error (m3/s)")
for (i in 1:3) {
  a <- c(0.9, 0.98, 0.995)[i]
  lines(lead, project(a, 1, steps), col = pal[i + 1], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topright", paste("a =", c(0.9, 0.98, 0.995)), col = pal[2:4], lwd = 2, bty = "n")

How an error of 1 m3/s is carried forward by AR(1) models, at 15-minute steps.

The time an error takes to fall to 37 per cent (1/e) of its size is its decay time: -1 / log(a) steps. For a = 0.98 that is 49 steps, about 12 hours at 15 minutes.

Three coefficients: the IMFS models

IMFS uses three coefficients, AR(3): the next error depends on the last three.

next error = a1 × current error + a2 × previous error + a3 × the one before

Three past values carry more than size. They also carry direction: whether the error is growing or shrinking. The Environment Agency 2024 default set is

ar_ea_default()
#>       a_1       a_2       a_3 
#>  1.765000 -0.726250 -0.040656

These numbers are hard to read directly, because they work together. Two views help.

What it does to a steady error, and to a growing one 

ea <- ar_ea_default()
steady <- project(ea, c(1, 1, 1), steps)
growing <- project(ea, c(1, 0.8, 0.6), steps)
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(range(lead), range(c(0, steady, growing)), type = "n", xlab = "Lead time (h)",
     ylab = "Predicted error (m3/s)")
lines(lead, steady, col = pal[2], lwd = 2)
lines(lead, growing, col = pal[3], lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("steady error", "growing error"), col = pal[2:3], lwd = 2, bty = "n")

The EA 2024 default projecting an error that has been steady at 1 m3/s, and one that has been growing (0.6, 0.8, then 1 m3/s).

A steady error of 1 m3/s fades slowly: 0.82 after 6 hours, 0.39 after a day. A growing error keeps growing for a while, to a peak of 1.69 m3/s about 3 hours ahead, before it too fades. The model extrapolates the recent trend in the error. On a rising limb where the model is falling further behind, that is exactly right. Where the error was growing because of gauge noise or a short blip, the AR model projects the blip forward. That is why the hindcast found it no better than persistence in the first hour on noisy data.

Roots: the timescales inside the model

An AR(3) model behaves like three simple fading processes added together, one for each root of its characteristic equation. Each root has its own decay time, and that splits the coefficients into timescales a hydrologist can read:

ar_roots <- function(a) {
  z <- polyroot(c(-rev(unname(a)), 1))
  data.frame(root = format(round(z, 4)), decay_steps = round(-1 / log(Mod(z)), 2),
             decay_hours_at_15min = round(-1 / log(Mod(z)) / 4, 2))
}
ar_roots(ea)
#>         root decay_steps decay_hours_at_15min
#> 1 -0.0498+0i        0.33                 0.08
#> 2  0.8252+0i        5.20                 1.30
#> 3  0.9896+0i       95.79                23.95

The EA default has:

  • a slow root, near 1, decaying over about a day: the persistence of the error;
  • a medium root, decaying in about five steps: this one carries the trend;
  • a tiny negative root, gone within a step: it only fine-tunes the first step.

The model is stable if every root lies strictly between -1 and 1 in size. A root of size 1 or more would make a projected error grow without limit. reach.postproc::assess() applies the Environment Agency’s review criteria to a parameter set, including stability, decay times that are too long or too short, and unwanted oscillation. Use it on any set before operational use.

Where coefficients come from

Source Function When
EA 2024 default ar_ea_default() No better information; defined for 15-minute steps
The default family, from one timescale ar_from_response_time() You know how fast the catchment responds; at steps longer than 15 minutes, only for a slow enough catchment (below)
Fitted to this model’s errors fit_error_updater(), or fit_window in pdm_hindcast() A long record of this model’s errors exists
Fitted to flood events only reach.postproc::fit_ar_from_events() Floods are what matter, and there are enough of them

The default family

The EA default is one member of a family of AR(3) sets, all sharing the same first coefficient and fast root, and differing only in the decay time of the slow root. ar_from_response_time() builds a member from one timescale, by the same construction as reach.postproc::default_family_ar_parameters(). pdmS7 offers the model’s own time to peak from pdm_response_time() as that timescale.

decays <- c(3, 12, 24, 96)
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(range(lead), c(0, 1), type = "n", xlab = "Lead time (h)",
     ylab = "Predicted error (m3/s)")
for (i in seq_along(decays)) {
  lines(lead, project(ar_from_response_time(decays[i], dt = 0.25), c(1, 1, 1), steps),
        col = pal[i + 1], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topright", paste(decays, "h"), col = pal[2:5], lwd = 2, bty = "n")

A steady error projected by members of the default family, labelled by their principal decay time, at 15-minute steps.

The EA 2024 default sits almost exactly on the 24-hour member. A flashy catchment, with a short time to peak, gets a correction that fades quickly; a slow one keeps its correction for longer. Linking the forecast error’s decay to the catchment’s time to peak is an approximation, the same one reach.postproc makes, so check the result with a hindcast.

Which timescale?

The family needs one timescale, and there are two candidates: the model’s own time to peak, from pdm_response_time(), and the response time estimated from the records alone by response_time_dmca() (Events in large samples). The second needs no model, but it measures the timescale of the fast response, which is usually shorter than the time to peak. Two things decide between them: whether the set is stable, and whether it forecasts well.

Stability. The family’s first coefficient, 1.765, is set for 15-minute steps. With a principal decay of too few steps, its second root reaches 1, and the projected error grows without limit. ar_from_response_time() refuses such a set.

shortest_steps <- -1 / log(1.765 - 1 + exp(-3))
c(shortest_decay_steps = round(shortest_steps, 2),
  at_15_minutes_h = round(shortest_steps * 0.25, 2), at_hourly_h = round(shortest_steps, 2))
#> shortest_decay_steps      at_15_minutes_h          at_hourly_h 
#>                 4.88                 1.22                 4.88
tryCatch(ar_from_response_time(3, dt = 1), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "The default-family AR set is unstable for a decay of 3 h at 1 h steps: one root is 1.1. The family is built for 15-minute steps and is stable only for a decay of at least 4.88 steps (4.88 h here). Use a finer step, a longer decay, ar_ea_default() or fitted coefficients."

At 15-minute steps the limit is 1.2 hours, which almost every catchment exceeds. At hourly steps it is 4.9 hours, and fast catchments fall below it. pdm_hindcast() leaves an unstable default set out, with a warning.

This catchment, at 15-minute steps. The two timescales, from the first half of the record, and hindcast skill against persistence over the second half:

half <- n / 2
high <- unname(stats::quantile(observed[seq_len(half)], 0.9))
time_to_peak <- pdm_response_time(model, flow = high)$time_to_peak_h
dmca <- response_time_dmca(rain[seq_len(half)], observed[seq_len(half)], dt = 0.25)$response_h
c(time_to_peak_h = round(time_to_peak, 2), dmca_h = dmca)
#> time_to_peak_h         dmca_h 
#>           2.78           2.00
compare <- pdm_hindcast(model, forcing, observed, window = (half + 1):n, every_h = 6,
                        horizon_h = 24, response_flow = high,
                        ar = list(time_to_peak = ar_from_response_time(time_to_peak, 0.25),
                                  dmca = ar_from_response_time(dmca, 0.25)))
compare_scores <- hindcast_scores(compare)
compare_scores <- compare_scores[compare_scores$lead_h %in% c(1, 3, 6, 12, 24) &
                                   compare_scores$method %in% c("time_to_peak", "dmca"), ]
skill <- data.table::dcast(data.table::as.data.table(compare_scores), lead_h ~ method,
                           value.var = "skill")
skill$difference <- skill$dmca - skill$time_to_peak
round(skill, 4)
#> Key: <lead_h>
#>    lead_h   dmca time_to_peak difference
#>     <num>  <num>        <num>      <num>
#> 1:      1 0.8720       0.8716      4e-04
#> 2:      3 0.9159       0.9151      7e-04
#> 3:      6 0.9393       0.9386      7e-04
#> 4:     12 0.9603       0.9601      2e-04
#> 5:     24 0.9658       0.9657      0e+00

The two sets forecast alike here: the skill differs by at most 0.0007 at any lead time.

A sample, at hourly steps. The same comparison over eight synthetic catchments with two years of hourly data each, calibrated automatically: both timescales from the calibration window, the hindcast over the validation window.

basins <- file.path(tempdir(), "ar-basins")
output <- file.path(tempdir(), "ar-projects")
unlink(c(basins, output), recursive = TRUE)
sample <- synthetic_basins(basins, n = 8, years = 2, dt = 1, seed = 21)
old <- options(pdmS7.user = "Ann Custodian", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
limited <- identical(toupper(Sys.getenv("_R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_")), "TRUE")
cores <- if (limited) 2L else min(4L, max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L))
status <- calibrate_batch(basins, output, starts = 2, control = list(maxit = 30),
                          cores = cores)
options(old)
stable_set <- function(h) tryCatch(ar_from_response_time(h, 1), error = function(e) NULL)
per_basin <- lapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  dir <- file.path(basins, id)
  f <- as.data.frame(data.table::fread(file.path(dir, "forcing.csv")))
  obs <- data.table::fread(file.path(dir, "flow.csv"))$q_m3s
  meta <- yaml::read_yaml(file.path(dir, "basin.yml"))
  day <- substr(f$time, 1, 10)
  cal <- match(meta$calibration[[1]], day):max(which(day == meta$calibration[[2]]))
  val <- match(meta$validation[[1]], day):max(which(day == meta$validation[[2]]))
  project <- file.path(output, id)
  fitted <- pdm_from_config(read_entry(project, read_projects(project)$candidate)$configuration)
  q90 <- unname(stats::quantile(obs[cal], 0.9, na.rm = TRUE))
  ttp <- suppressWarnings(pdm_response_time(fitted, flow = q90))$time_to_peak_h
  dm <- response_time_dmca(f$rain[cal], obs[cal], dt = 1)$response_h
  sets <- Filter(Negate(is.null), list(time_to_peak = stable_set(ttp), dmca = stable_set(dm)))
  out <- data.frame(basin = id, time_to_peak_h = round(ttp, 1), dmca_h = dm,
                    time_to_peak_stable = !is.null(sets$time_to_peak),
                    dmca_stable = !is.null(sets$dmca), change_3h = NA, change_12h = NA,
                    change_24h = NA)
  if (length(sets) == 2) {
    hc <- suppressWarnings(pdm_hindcast(fitted, f, obs, window = val, every_h = 6,
                                        horizon_h = 24, ar = sets, response_flow = q90))
    sc <- hindcast_scores(hc)
    at <- function(m, h) sc$skill[sc$method == m & sc$lead_h == h]
    out[c("change_3h", "change_12h", "change_24h")] <- vapply(c(3, 12, 24), function(h) {
      at("dmca", h) - at("time_to_peak", h)
    }, numeric(1))
  }
  out
})
by_basin <- do.call(rbind, per_basin)
by_basin[c("change_3h", "change_12h", "change_24h")] <-
  round(by_basin[c("change_3h", "change_12h", "change_24h")], 4)
by_basin
#>   basin time_to_peak_h dmca_h time_to_peak_stable dmca_stable change_3h
#> 1  S001           19.5     11                TRUE        TRUE    0.0001
#> 2  S002            6.8      4                TRUE       FALSE        NA
#> 3  S003            9.0      5                TRUE        TRUE   -0.0004
#> 4  S004            4.3      2               FALSE       FALSE        NA
#> 5  S005           16.4      9                TRUE        TRUE   -0.0002
#> 6  S006           33.1     18                TRUE        TRUE   -0.0011
#> 7  S007            3.9      2               FALSE       FALSE        NA
#> 8  S008            5.2      3                TRUE       FALSE        NA
#>   change_12h change_24h
#> 1     0.0008    -0.0017
#> 2         NA         NA
#> 3    -0.0035    -0.0046
#> 4         NA         NA
#> 5    -0.0012    -0.0085
#> 6     0.0051    -0.0084
#> 7         NA         NA
#> 8         NA         NA

The response time from the records is typically 55 per cent of the time to peak. At hourly steps that matters more than anything else: the set built on it is unstable, and refused, in 4 of the 8 catchments, against 2 for the time to peak. Where both sets are stable (4 catchments), the change in skill is small, and at a 24-hour lead the set built on the records’ response time is worse in 4 of them.

So the model’s time to peak remains the timescale to use. The records’ response time is no better where both work, and fails more often at hourly steps. For a fast catchment at hourly steps, neither works: use fitted coefficients, or run the model at 15-minute steps, where the family was built.

Fitting

fit_error_updater() fits the coefficients to a model’s errors by maximum likelihood, using stats::arima():

calibration <- seq_len(n / 2)
fitted <- fit_error_updater(observed[calibration], simulated[calibration], order = c(3, 0))
#> Maximum likelihood failed; the AR fit used method CSS-ML
round(fitted$updater@ar, 4)
#> [1]  1.2200  0.2375 -0.4676
ar_roots(fitted$updater@ar)
#>         root decay_steps decay_hours_at_15min
#> 1  0.8396+0i        5.72                 1.43
#> 2 -0.5799+0i        1.84                 0.46
#> 3  0.9602+0i       24.65                 6.16

Exact maximum likelihood failed on this series, so the fit fell back to method CSS-ML, as the message says; the coefficients are still a proper fit.

The fitted set is quite unlike the default. Its slowest root decays over about 6 hours, against the default’s 24, and one root is clearly negative, which makes part of the projected error flip sign from step to step. A shorter decay than the default says this model’s errors fade faster than the default assumes; part of the reason is gauge noise, which pulls a fit towards fast decay (below). reach.postproc::assess() would test both the decay time and any oscillation against the review criteria.

A fit reflects this model’s errors, in this catchment, over this period. It changes whenever the model is recalibrated. A fit over a whole record is weighted towards quiet weather, because there is more of it, and gauge noise pulls the coefficients towards fast decay. Fitting to flood events only, as reach.postproc::fit_ar_from_events() does, targets the conditions that matter. Whichever you use, judge it on events it was not fitted to.

Sign conventions

The same model can be written with opposite signs, and mixing them up turns a stable model into an unstable one. pdmS7 follows IMFS, Deltares and reach.postproc:

Convention Written as EA 2024 default
Deltares, IMFS, reach.postproc, pdmS7 next error = a1 × current + a2 × previous + a3 × earlier a = 1.765, -0.72625, -0.040656
Moore (2007), equation 31 coefficients phi = -a phi = -1.765, 0.72625, 0.040656

error_updater(ar = ) takes the Deltares values, so a set can be copied from IMFS or reach.postproc unchanged.

ARMA: adding a moving average

An ARMA model adds moving-average (MA) terms: the next error also depends on recent surprises, the parts of recent errors the AR terms did not predict. They let the model react to a sudden change, such as a shift in the rating, without the long memory of the AR part. pdmS7 supports them, with error_updater(ar = , ma = ) and fit_error_updater(order = c(p, q)), and Moore (2007) describes them, but IMFS uses AR only. Start with AR(3); add an MA term only if a hindcast shows it helps.

arma <- fit_error_updater(observed[calibration], simulated[calibration], order = c(2, 1))
c(ar = round(arma$updater@ar, 3), ma = round(arma$updater@ma, 3))
#>    ar1    ar2     ma 
#>  1.251 -0.256  0.138

Additive or log errors

By default errors are in m3/s, additive, as in IMFS. With scale = "log" they are taken on the log scale, so a 10 per cent error at high flow counts the same as a 10 per cent error at low flow, and a correction can never make the flow negative. Additive correction can push a low flow below zero; pdm_hindcast() raises any updated flow below lower_limit, 0 by default, back up to it.

Where AR correction stops working

AR correction predicts how the error develops. It does not know about the river. So:

  • Timing errors. If the model’s flood arrives an hour late, the error swings positive then negative. The AR model sees only the first half and projects it forward, the wrong way.
  • Noise. Gauge noise in the latest observation is projected forward as if it were real.
  • Gaps. With a missing observation in the last three steps, there is no projection; the hindcast leaves that origin out.
  • Ratings. A correction made in flow does not keep its shape when converted to level through a nonlinear rating, and the reverse.
  • Beyond the decay time, the correction has faded and the forecast is the model’s alone.

The way to know whether it helps, and at which lead times, is to test it on past events: Testing forecasts with hindcasts.

Summary

Question Answer
What is corrected? The error, observed minus simulated, projected forward from the forecast origin
What do the coefficients mean? Read them through their roots: each root is a decay time
Which set? Start from the EA 2024 default or ar_from_response_time(); fit only with care
Is it stable? Every root smaller than 1 in size; check with reach.postproc::assess()
Does it help here? Run pdm_hindcast() and compare skill against persistence by lead time
